name: The Ehrlich-Simon wager
scope: A scientific argument settled by a bet, and the loser paid. T1: in October 1990 the biologist Paul Ehrlich mailed the economist Julian Simon a cheque for $576.07 -- the hook is that a public quarrel about the fate of humanity was resolved by a WAGER with a settlement date. T1: Simon let Ehrlich pick the terms -- any raw materials, any span longer than a year -- which is what turned an argument into a genuine test rather than a stunt. T2: Ehrlich and his colleagues chose five metals: copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten, formalised 29 September 1980 with payoff on 29 September 1990, $1,000 staked as $200 per metal. T2: 'cheaper' was defined precisely -- the INFLATION-ADJUSTED cost, using the US Consumer Price Index, of buying the same QUANTITIES ten years later (teach real vs nominal price before testing it). T2: the prophecy under test was the opening line of Ehrlich's 1968 bestseller The Population Bomb, published by Sierra Club Books: 'The battle to feed all of humanity is over. In the 1970s hundreds of millions of people will starve to death in spite of any crash programs embarked upon now.' T3: tin fell from $8.72 a pound to $3.88; tin and tungsten each dropped over 60% in real terms, and every one of the five metals cost less in 1990 than in 1980. T3: the whole basket that cost $1,000 in 1980 cost roughly $424 to reassemble in 1990 -- a 57.6% real decline, which is where the odd figure $576.07 comes from. T3: Simon's mechanism, argued in The Ultimate Resource (1981) -- a rising price is not a countdown, it is a SIGNAL that pays people to find substitutes, work leaner ore, recycle and use less; his claim was that the ultimate resource is people, because more people means more problem-solvers. T4: Ehrlich's reaction -- he told the New York Times in December 1990 'the bet doesn't mean anything', and told the BBC it had been 'an excellent bet' that his side 'happened to lose'. T4: the STEEL-MAN -- 1980 metal prices sat near a cyclical peak just before a global recession, and critics argue the window flattered Simon; run the same wager across other decades and Simon wins more often than not, but not always. One decade is one trial, not a law. T4: the rematch nobody made -- Simon offered $10,000 or more on any commodities over any span of five years or longer; Ehrlich and the climatologist Stephen Schneider countered in 1995 with fifteen environmental 'indicators of material change' instead of prices; Simon refused those as indirect and insisted on human-welfare measures such as life expectancy, infant mortality and food per head. No second bet was ever struck, and Simon died in February 1998. T5: the same year he mailed the cheque, 1990, Ehrlich received a MacArthur Prize Fellowship and the Crafoord Prize from the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. A failed prophecy cost its author nothing -- prestige and accuracy are awarded separately, and noticing that gap is the skill.
source: Grokipedia 'Simon-Ehrlich wager' (read via browser; Grokipedia returns 403 to direct fetch) -- bet terms, CPI methodology, 57.6% real decline, per-metal price changes, Ehrlich's BBC/NYT reactions, the unexecuted second wager and the 1995 Ehrlich-Schneider counterproposal. Wikipedia 'Simon-Ehrlich wager' (dates, $576.07, tin/chromium nominal prices), 'The Population Bomb' (opening sentence, publisher, India claims, Ehrlich's 2009 partial retraction), 'Paul R. Ehrlich' (1990 MacArthur Fellowship and Crafoord Prize; the 1970 Earth Day and 1971 England predictions).
framing_note: FLAGSHIP of the sub-strand and one of its two T1-T2 load-bearers -- open on the ACT (a cheque in the post) and the FAIRNESS (Ehrlich chose the metals), never on a date. ACCURACY RAIL, non-negotiable: the bet was on INFLATION-ADJUSTED prices of fixed quantities, not nominal prices, and Simon did not predict prices would fall -- he bet they would not RISE in real terms; Ehrlich paid promptly and in full, so no rung may imply he welshed. Second rail: state the steel-man rung honestly -- the 1980 starting point was near a cyclical peak, and the bank's own case is stronger for admitting it. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (the cheque) and T5 (the prizes in the same year). DISTRACTOR MINE: real rival scarcity claims and their real authors -- Malthus's 1798 essay, Hubbert's peak, the Club of Rome's exhaustion table, Garrett Hardin, John Holdren; plus other real metals (aluminium, zinc, silver, cobalt) and real wrong settlement figures. Never a joke option. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem say 'the metals got cheaper' before asking who won -- describe the wager, the ten-year clock and the envelope, and let the outcome be recalled knowledge. TONE: no gloating. Ehrlich was a serious scientist making a serious argument that failed a test he agreed to take; that is the whole lesson and it dies if the voice sneers. LANE: ECONOMICS bank owns price theory, substitution and Simon-as-economist; HISTORY owns 1970s politics; SCIENCE keeps the WAGER-AS-TEST and the graded prediction record.
history_overlap: ECONOMICS bank -- very likely covers Julian Simon, The Ultimate Resource, Malthus and the resource-scarcity argument as economics; this ladder must key the BET as an experimental protocol (who chose the metals, what 'cheaper' was defined as, the settlement arithmetic) and the prediction record, NOT price theory. Also check the science bank's own climate sub-strand, which names failed predictions including Ehrlich's famines -- that must not be re-told here.

name: The prophecy's price: sterilisation quotas and the one-child policy
scope: What happens when a population forecast acquires the authority of science and the power of a state. T2: between 1976 and 1977 India performed 8.3 million sterilisations, most of them coerced, up from 2.7 million the year before -- a single year's campaign run during Indira Gandhi's Emergency and driven by her son Sanjay Gandhi from September 1976. T2: what The Population Bomb actually recommended -- Ehrlich's 1968 book urged compulsory sterilisation of Indian men with three or more children and proposed the United States supply helicopters and surgical instruments to support the vasectomy programme. The recommendation is in the book; this is not an inference. T3: how a quota works -- targets were handed down to officials, teachers and clerks who were paid or threatened by them, and police delivered people to sterilisation camps; the mechanism that produced the number was the number itself. T3: Muzaffarnagar, 18 October 1976 -- police detained seventeen people for sterilisation, a crowd resisted, and roughly thirty people died. T3: the reckoning -- 'nasbandi' became the grievance that broke the Emergency; Congress lost the March 1977 election and Indira Gandhi lost her own seat. A coerced policy was ended by a vote, which is the one control the planners had not modelled. T3: China's one-child policy was formally implemented on 18 September 1980 and was not replaced until 1 January 2016. T4: Song Jian, a Chinese control engineer trained on missile-guidance mathematics, read The Limits to Growth while visiting Europe in 1980, ran China's population through control-theory equations, and his group concluded at the 1980 Chengdu meeting that the country's 'ideal' population was 700 million -- a target that required universal one-child restrictions. T4: THE HONEST CAVEAT -- scholars including Wang Feng and colleagues dispute how much Song's models mattered, showing that Party leaders had already settled on one-child restrictions in 1979, before Song's work reached them. The equations may have supplied AUTHORITY rather than the decision, which is its own lesson. T4: the machinery, in numbers -- between 1980 and 2014 some 324 million women received IUDs and 108 million were sterilised, with 'social maintenance fees' on unauthorised births running to one to three years of a family's income. T5: the arithmetic that came back -- China's sex ratio at birth rose from about 108 boys per 100 girls in 1981 to about 117 per 100 by 2000, leaving an estimated 32 to 36 million more men than women in those cohorts. T5: the Party credits the policy with preventing 400 million births, a figure scholars dispute; the deeper point is that no planner in either country ever had to name a date and be graded the way Simon and Ehrlich graded each other. The forecasts were enforced, not tested.
source: Wikipedia 'The Emergency (India)' (Sanjay Gandhi's September 1976 campaign; 8.3 million sterilisations in 1976-77 against 2.7 million the prior year; quotas and police involvement; the Muzaffarnagar incident of 18 October 1976 and ~30 deaths; the nasbandi grievance and the March 1977 defeat). Wikipedia 'One-child policy' (implementation 18 September 1980, replacement 1 January 2016; Song Jian, his 1980 reading of The Limits to Growth in Europe, the Chengdu meeting and the 700-million target; the Wang et al. dispute over Song's primacy; 324 million IUD insertions and 108 million sterilisations 1980-2014; social maintenance fees; sex ratio 108:100 in 1981 to 117:100 by 2000 and 32-36 million excess males; the disputed 400-million-births-prevented claim). Wikipedia 'The Population Bomb' (Ehrlich's explicit endorsement of compulsory sterilisation in India and of US logistical support for vasectomy programmes).
framing_note: THE MORAL CORE of the sub-strand -- the 'anti-human turn' is not a slogan here, it is a documented record of coercion, and the ladder must let the NUMBERS and the absence of consent carry every ounce of the weight. TONE RAIL, strictest in the sub-strand (audience is 10 to 15): state the record plainly and clinically; no graphic surgical or medical detail, no dwelling on suffering. Name the wrong precisely as COERCION -- people were sterilised who did not agree -- and do NOT open any adjacent argument about family size, contraception or abortion as such; those are not this ladder's subject and a stray editorial line would wreck it. ACCURACY RAIL: the T4 caveat rung is MANDATORY and may not be softened or dropped -- historians genuinely dispute whether Song Jian's models caused the one-child policy or merely dressed a decision the Party had already taken in 1979. A ladder about the misuse of scientific authority cannot itself overstate a causal chain; if the build cannot source both sides, it must cut the Song rungs rather than assert the strong version. Also: Ehrlich RECOMMENDED compulsory sterilisation in print, but do not claim he caused India's campaign -- the honest claim is that a scientist's prestige was lent to coercion, not that he ordered it. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (8.3 million in one year) and T3 (the election that ended it -- the ladder must not leave kids without the fact that people voted it down). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent population figures and programmes -- Malthus, Garrett Hardin, the Club of Rome, Sanjay Gandhi versus Indira Gandhi, Chen Yun, the wan-xi-shao campaign, Zero Population Growth; real wrong years (1975 vs 1976 vs 1980) and real wrong magnitudes. VERIFY BEFORE SEEDING: any rung on foreign funding or pressure (World Bank, USAID, Ford Foundation, Sweden) was NOT verified at spec time -- source it or drop it. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem announce 'quotas caused mass coerced sterilisation' before asking what happened -- describe the camps, the targets and the year, and let the number be recalled. LANE: HISTORY owns the Emergency as a political episode and the CCP as governance; SCIENCE keeps only the SCIENTIFIC-AUTHORITY chain -- what the book recommended, what the model computed, and who was never graded.
history_overlap: HISTORY bank -- the Indian Emergency 1975-77 (Indira and Sanjay Gandhi, the suspension of civil liberties, the 1977 election) and China's one-child policy as CCP governance are near-certain history topics; this ladder must key the SCIENTIFIC-AUTHORITY chain only (Ehrlich's printed recommendation, Song Jian's control-theory model and the scholarly dispute over it) and hand the elections, the Emergency's politics and Party history to history. Also flag against this bank's own eugenics/dark-chapters ladder -- coerced sterilisation appears there via Buck v. Bell and California; those are DIFFERENT facts and neither ladder may borrow the other's cases.

name: Limits to Growth and the deadlines that expired
scope: A computer model read as a prophecy, and the honest scorecard. T2: The Limits to Growth appeared on 2 March 1972, written by Donella Meadows, Dennis Meadows, Jorgen Randers and William Behrens with a seventeen-person MIT team, commissioned by a private association of businessmen and scientists called the Club of Rome, and it sold roughly 30 million copies in 30 languages -- the best-selling environmental book ever printed. T2: the machine behind it was a computer model named World3 with five interacting dials: population, food production, industrialisation, pollution, and consumption of non-renewable resources. T3: THE TABLE everyone remembers -- the book printed exhaustion figures for nineteen non-renewable resources, and at then-current growth rates petroleum ran out in 20 years and lead in 21, putting oil's expiry at 1992. T3: the sentence the popular retelling dropped -- the authors wrote that their figures were predictions 'only in the most limited sense of the word'; the table was arithmetic demonstrating what exponential growth does to any fixed number, not a forecast the model had produced. The failure was as much in the reading as the writing, and the bank says so. T3: the modelling choice that did the damage, named by the economists Allen Kneese and Ronald Riker in 1973 -- resources and pollution were allowed to grow exponentially while technological improvement grew only linearly. Let one curve bend and not the other and collapse is baked in before the machine starts. T4: M. King Hubbert's 1956 paper predicted that United States oil production would peak between 1965 and 1970. It peaked in 1970 at 10.2 million barrels a day, and stayed within ten per cent of his curve from 1974 to 1994. He was RIGHT, and the ladder says so plainly. T4: Hubbert's other prediction -- a world peak about half a century from 1956, so around 2006 -- missed, and by November 2017 the United States alone was back above 10 million barrels a day. T4: WHY it missed, the mechanism -- hydraulic fracturing combined with horizontal drilling turned the impermeable source rock that oil is BORN in into something you can produce from, so the resource base is not a tank being drained but a function of what people know how to do. T4: the contemporary criticism -- Peter Passell called the model 'garbage in, garbage out' in the New York Times in 1972, and the Sussex Science Policy Research Unit showed in 1973 that the collapse could be tuned away by changing assumptions the model itself could not test. T5: the fair-minded rung -- Graham Turner in 2008 and Gaya Herrington in 2020 compared decades of real-world data against the book's standard run and found it tracking; that scenario's collapse is dated to the middle-to-late twenty-first century and has therefore not been tested yet. Honest people are still watching. T5: the recognition skill -- a model is a hypothesis with arithmetic attached, and it earns belief the way any hypothesis does: by making a dated, falsifiable call and surviving it. Hubbert made two and split them; the resource table made one and expired.
source: Wikipedia 'The Limits to Growth' (publication 2 March 1972, the four named authors and 17-person team, Club of Rome commission, ~30 million copies in 30 languages; World3's five variables and the exponential-versus-linear assumption; the 19-resource table with petroleum at 20 years and lead at 21 under exponential growth; the authors' own 'only in the most limited sense of the word' disclaimer; Passell's 1972 'garbage in, garbage out', the 1973 Sussex SPRU sensitivity critique, Kneese and Riker 1973; Turner 2008 and Herrington 2020 finding the standard run tracking). Wikipedia 'Hubbert peak theory' (the 1956 paper's two scenarios -- most likely peak 1965 at 150 Gb, upper bound 1970 at 200 Gb; the actual 1970 peak at 10.2 million barrels/day and the 1974-1994 fit; the global peak of about half a century out, i.e. ~2006; tight oil and the return above 10 million barrels/day by November 2017).
framing_note: THE central accuracy rail, and the reason this ladder is hard to write well: do NOT say 'Limits to Growth predicted the world would run out of oil in 1992.' The book's own text disclaimed the table as prediction, and the T3 disclaimer rung is MANDATORY. The honest and far more interesting charge is that the table was widely READ as prophecy -- including, on the record, by Song Jian in 1980 -- and that the standard run's collapse remains untested. No rung may imply the authors lied or that the model has been refuted; the Turner/Herrington rung exists precisely to stop that and may not be cut. Equally, the Hubbert rung where he was RIGHT is load-bearing: a ladder that only dunks teaches contempt, not method, and Hubbert is the proof that a dated forecast can succeed. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the same man called America's peak to the year and missed the world's completely). DISTRACTOR MINE: real rival forecasters and real models -- Malthus, Hubbert, Julian Simon, Garrett Hardin, the Global 2000 Report to the President (1980), the Club of Rome versus the Bilderberg Group versus the Royal Society (real, confusable institutions); real wrong years for the oil column (1982, 1992, 2002) and real other resources from the table (chromium, lead, natural gas). VERIFY BEFORE SEEDING: (a) any claim about proved oil reserves being LARGER in 1992 than 1972 was not verified at spec time -- source it or phrase the rung around the fact that the column simply expired; (b) W. S. Jevons's 1865 coal panic is a strong extra distractor or rung but was not verified here. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem say 'the deadlines passed' before asking what the table forecast -- give the year, the book and the resource count, and let the number be recalled. TEACH BEFORE TESTING: define exponential versus linear growth in a T2 rung before any rung leans on the distinction. LANE: GEOGRAPHY owns oil fields as places and the geology tour; ECONOMICS owns resource economics and price signals; SCIENCE keeps model-versus-test epistemology and the fracking mechanism.
history_overlap: ECONOMICS bank -- resource scarcity, peak oil and the Club of Rome are plausible economics topics; keep this ladder on the MODEL's construction and its falsifiability record. GEOGRAPHY bank -- likely tours oil-producing regions and may carry a shale entry; this ladder keys the DRILLING MECHANISM and the failed forecast, not the places. Also flag against the Ehrlich-Simon ladder in this same sub-strand: the Club of Rome may be named there as a distractor but its table belongs only here.

name: Borlaug's dwarf wheat and the famine that did not come
scope: The specific plant-breeding trick that broke the prophecy, told as a discovery. T1: tall wheat given plenty of fertiliser grows a head so heavy the stalk falls over and the grain rots on the ground -- farmers call it lodging. Norman Borlaug's answer was to make the wheat SHORTER, so a stubby thick stem could hold a far bigger head upright. Less plant, more bread. T1: the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize went to a plant breeder, and when the call came Borlaug thought the whole thing was a hoax. T2: the dwarfing genes were not his -- they came from a Japanese variety called Norin 10, which he got hold of in 1953 and crossed into disease-resistant lines to produce cultivars such as Pitic 62 and Penjamo 62. T2: shuttle breeding -- from 1945 Borlaug broke the rule that you get one wheat generation a year by hauling seed roughly 700 miles between a highland station and the Valle del Yaqui near Ciudad Obregon, at different altitudes and latitudes, harvesting two generations a year and halving the time to a finished variety. T3: THE ACCIDENT WORTH MORE THAN THE SPEED -- because the seed was being selected at two different latitudes at once, the surviving lines came out photoperiod-INSENSITIVE, meaning they did not care how long the day was and would therefore grow almost anywhere. A shortcut taken to save time produced a property nobody was aiming at, which is what field tests do to plans. T3: the numbers set against the forecast -- Ehrlich wrote in 1968 that he could not see how India could feed two hundred million more people by 1980; India's wheat harvest went from 12.3 million tonnes in 1965 to 20.1 million in 1970, Pakistan's from 4.6 to 7.3 million over the same years, and India was self-sufficient in all cereals by 1974. Mexico's 1963 harvest was six times its 1944 harvest and the country had become a wheat exporter. T4: the famous figure needs a footnote -- 'Borlaug saved a billion lives' is an ESTIMATE, first put into print by the journalist Gregg Easterbrook in a 1997 article titled 'Forgotten Benefactor of Humanity', and echoed by the agricultural economist Dennis Avery; in 2009 the World Food Programme's Josette Sheeran said he 'saved more lives than any man in human history'. It is a defensible estimate, not a measurement, and the bank checks its own heroes. T5: Borlaug's own verdict -- in his 1970 Nobel lecture he warned of 'the frightening power of human reproduction', insisted there are 'no miracles in agricultural production', and said that unless yields kept rising the coming century would see misery exceeding anything before it. The man who broke the prophecy refused to declare the problem solved.
source: Wikipedia 'Norman Borlaug' (Norin 10 acquired 1953 and crossed with Brevor 14; semi-dwarf stems and lodging; Pitic 62 and Penjamo 62; shuttle breeding from 1945 between the central highlands and the Valle del Yaqui near Ciudad Obregon, ~700 miles, and the unplanned photoperiod-insensitivity; Mexico 95% semi-dwarf by 1963 and a 1963 harvest six times 1944; India 12.3 Mt in 1965 to 20.1 Mt in 1970 and 76.4 Mt by 2000; Pakistan 4.6 Mt to 7.3 Mt and self-sufficiency by 1968; India self-sufficient in all cereals by 1974; the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize and his belief it was a hoax; the 'billion lives' figure traced to Gregg Easterbrook's 1997 'Forgotten Benefactor of Humanity' and Dennis Avery, plus Josette Sheeran's 2009 statement; his 'no miracles in agricultural production' line and 1970 Nobel lecture warnings). Wikipedia 'The Population Bomb' (Ehrlich's India claim).
framing_note: The sub-strand's POSITIVE pole and, with the Ehrlich-Simon ladder, its main T1-T2 wonder load -- this set skews analytic, so Borlaug must carry genuinely picture-able rungs. Open on the MECHANISM a ten-year-old can see: a fat wheat head snaps a tall stalk, so make the stalk short. ACCURACY RAIL: 'saved a billion lives' must be ATTRIBUTED, never asserted -- the T4 rung exists to name Easterbrook 1997 as the origin and to mark it an estimate. A bank that teaches kids to check claims cannot launder its own favourite statistic. Second rail: Borlaug did not invent dwarf wheat; the dwarfing genes came from Norin 10, and shuttle breeding was the method, not the gene. Third rail: he is a hero here, not a saint -- the T5 rung uses his OWN warnings, and the build should add the honest cost column (irrigation drawdown, fertiliser runoff, monoculture risk -- VERIFY and source before seeding) rather than presenting the Green Revolution as free. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a shortcut for speed accidentally produced wheat that grows anywhere) -- also the ladder's purest test-it-yourself moment, because the field, not the plan, taught him. DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent agricultural science -- hybrid maize (Shull, Wallace), Haber-Bosch nitrogen fixation, IR8 rice at IRRI, Mendel's peas, crop rotation, and Lysenko's vernalisation as the deliberate anti-example; real other Nobel categories and real wrong years. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem say 'shorter stems resist lodging' before asking what Borlaug bred for -- describe the fallen crop and the rotting grain and let the trait be recalled. LANE: COOKING owns wheat as flour, bread and diet; GEOGRAPHY owns the Punjab and the Yaqui Valley as places; SCIENCE keeps the BREEDING mechanism, the shuttle-breeding method and the falsified-forecast record.
history_overlap: COOKING bank -- wheat, flour and bread are certain cooking topics and the Green Revolution may appear there as a food-history entry; this ladder must key Norin 10, shuttle breeding and photoperiod insensitivity, never bread. GEOGRAPHY bank -- may tour the Punjab or Mexican agriculture. Within this science bank, flag against any genetics/Mendel ladder: Mendel's peas are the ancestor of this work but belong to that ladder, and the two must not share a rung.

name: Rule by the experts: Technocracy Inc. to Ostrom's canals
scope: A theme ladder on the planner's blind spot, deepened across named cases. T2: in the winter of 1932-33, with a quarter of America out of work, a movement briefly outran every other proposal for fixing the Depression by promising to abolish politicians, businessmen and money itself and hand the continent to engineers. It was called Technocracy. T2: Howard Scott's replacement for the dollar was the 'energy certificate' -- a citizen's ration measured in units of energy rather than currency, tracked by a continental accounting system covering all production and consumption. T3: how it died, in one night -- Scott's nationally broadcast address from the Hotel Pierre on 13 January 1933 met near-unanimous press ridicule, the American Engineering Council condemned the technocrats for 'unprofessional activity', and the mass movement never recovered. A plan for a continent did not survive its own first radio speech. T3: the earliest warning was in the movement's own history -- Scott's Technical Alliance, founded in New York in late 1919, set out to survey all the energy in North America and dissolved in 1921 without finishing. The data a planner needs can be bigger than the planner. T3: Garrett Hardin's 1968 essay in Science set the problem in a parable -- a shared pasture, each herdsman rationally adding one more cow because he takes the whole gain and shares the cost, and ruin arriving as arithmetic. T4: what the parable quietly assumed -- Hardin's herdsmen cannot talk to each other. Real people sharing a resource talk, watch, and punish, and that single missing feature is the difference between a thought experiment and a law of nature. T4: Elinor Ostrom's method was to stop arguing and go look -- she and her students studied the actual rules of actual places: Swiss alpine pastures, Japanese village forests, the huerta irrigation canals of Spain, Philippine zanjera systems, Nepali irrigation in Dang Deukhuri, fisheries in Nova Scotia and Indonesia. T4: the mechanism she kept finding was GRADUATED SANCTIONS -- the users monitor each other, and a first offence draws a small penalty rather than expulsion, so enforcement stays cheap, local and survivable. T4: in 2009 Ostrom shared the Nobel Prize in economics with Oliver Williamson, the first woman ever to win it, for showing that Hardin's tragedy is a possibility rather than a certainty. T5: her eight design principles for commons that last -- clear boundaries; rules matched to local conditions; the users themselves making the rules; monitoring; graduated sanctions; cheap conflict resolution; outside authorities recognising the right to organise; and nested layers for large systems. T5: the STEEL-MAN -- open-access resources with no community and no rules, such as distant-water fisheries or the atmosphere, really do behave the way Hardin described. Ostrom's finding was 'it depends on the institution', not 'Hardin was wrong', and the bank states it that way. T5: the through-line -- Friedrich Hayek argued in 1945 that the knowledge a central planner would need is dispersed, local and often unwritten; Ostrom's canals are that argument with a field notebook attached. The recognition skill: when someone proposes to run a system from above, ask what the people already running it know that the plan does not.
source: Wikipedia 'Technocracy movement' (Howard Scott; the Technical Alliance founded late 1919 in New York and dissolved 1921 with its North American energy survey unfinished; the Columbia Committee on Technocracy 1932 under Scott and Walter Rautenstrauch; the January 1933 split into Technocracy Incorporated and Harold Loeb's Continental Committee; the 16 June 1932 to 13 January 1933 peak of public attention; energy certificates and the energy theory of value; the Hotel Pierre broadcast of 13 January 1933, the press ridicule and the American Engineering Council's 'unprofessional activity' condemnation; the Continental Committee's collapse in October 1936). Wikipedia 'Elinor Ostrom' (the 2009 Nobel shared with Oliver Williamson and the first-woman fact; the citation for 'analysis of economic governance, especially the commons'; her field cases -- Spanish huerta, Swiss alpine pastures, Japanese village forests, Philippine zanjera, Nova Scotia and Indonesian fisheries, Nepali irrigation in Dang Deukhuri; the eight design principles; Hardin's 1968 herdsman parable and how cooperation, monitoring and enforcement avoid the tragedy).
framing_note: The ANALYTIC BACKBONE of the sub-strand -- a shape-B concept ladder carrying its own T4/T5 ceiling, so it may run light on T1 and let Borlaug and the Ehrlich-Simon ladder cover the easy end. The recognition skill it teaches is positive and testable: go and look at what already works before you replace it. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) Technocracy Incorporated still exists as a tiny organisation -- write 'collapsed as a mass movement', never 'vanished'; (2) Ostrom did NOT prove that commons always self-govern, nor that privatisation or state control is always wrong -- she proved a third option exists and identified the conditions under which it holds, and the steel-man rung on open-access resources is MANDATORY to keep the ladder honest; (3) Hardin's essay is a real and serious piece of work, not a joke -- present the parable at full strength before naming what it assumed. VERIFY BEFORE SEEDING: (a) Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society', American Economic Review, September 1945 -- confident but not verified at spec time, so source the citation or drop the rung; (b) the specific long-lived case Ostrom is famous for (Toerbel in Valais, with grazing rules recorded from 1483; the Valencia water tribunal's roughly thousand-year run) would make an excellent T3 but neither date was verified here -- verify or use the general finding; (c) the claim that outside intervention destroyed working local systems is standard in the literature but unsourced at spec time. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a plan to run North America by engineers, killed by one radio broadcast) and T4 (the herdsmen who could not talk). DISTRACTOR MINE: real rival planning ideas and their real authors -- Soviet Gosplan, the socialist calculation debate (Mises and Lange), Taylorism and scientific management, the New Deal's NRA, Pigou's taxes, Malthus, and Hardin's own 'mutual coercion mutually agreed upon'; real confusable Nobel laureates and real other design-principle counts. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem state that users can govern a commons before asking what Ostrom found -- describe her walking the canals and reading village rulebooks, and let the finding be recalled. LANE: ECONOMICS bank owns the knowledge problem, the calculation debate and Ostrom-as-economist outright; SCIENCE keeps the EPISTEMOLOGY -- armchair model versus field notebook, and 'go and look' as method. HISTORY owns the Great Depression.
history_overlap: ECONOMICS bank -- heavy and near-certain overlap: Hayek's knowledge problem, the socialist calculation debate, Ostrom's Nobel and the tragedy of the commons are core Bastiat-Pattern economics territory. This ladder must key the METHOD contrast (an untested parable versus decades of fieldwork) and the Technocracy episode, and must NOT re-argue price signals or central planning as economics. HISTORY bank -- the Great Depression and the New Deal; take only the Technocracy episode itself.

name: Davos: Schwab, the Great Reset, and the sentence nobody wrote as a plan
scope: A quote-provenance ladder: what was actually published, by whom, and in what form. T2: what Davos actually is -- in January 1971 a German engineering professor invited about four hundred European chief executives to a Swiss ski town for a management symposium; that meeting, held 24-26 January 1971, became the European Management Forum and, in 1987, the World Economic Forum. T2: the man -- Klaus Schwab holds a doctorate in engineering from ETH Zurich (1966) and a doctorate in economics from Fribourg (1967), plus a Harvard public-administration degree, where Henry Kissinger was among his professors. An engineer, not a banker. T3: THE SENTENCE -- 'I own nothing, have no privacy, and life has never been better' is not a leaked plan and not Schwab's words. It is the title of a 2016 essay the WEF published, written by Ida Auken, a Danish member of parliament sitting on a WEF council on cities, imagining life in 2030. The answer is a named Danish MP writing speculative fiction. T3: what Auken said afterwards -- she appended a note that the piece 'merely represented a potential future scenario' meant to 'start a discussion about pros and cons' of technological development, and the article was retitled 'Here's how life could change in my city by the year 2030'. T4: the Fourth Industrial Revolution -- Schwab's January 2016 Davos theme, article and book, arguing that a fusion of the physical, digital and biological spheres was arriving and would demand new forms of governance. This is his own signed thesis, published under his own name. T4: the Great Reset was launched in June 2020 and published as a book, COVID-19: The Great Reset, co-written with Thierry Malleret and released on 9 July 2020, arguing the pandemic was an opening to restructure economies around stakeholder capitalism and public-private coordination. A programme with an author's name on the cover -- which is exactly why it can be quoted accurately. T5: the objection that actually holds -- the WEF commands no votes and no army, but it convenes the people who command both, and the serious criticism of it is DEMOCRATIC rather than conspiratorial: unelected conveners shaping agendas no electorate approved, and doing it in public. T5: the discipline rung -- the widely repeated claim that Schwab's father was a Nazi collaborator has been examined and found unsubstantiated; the family firm's German subsidiary did supply the regime, but the personal allegations do not check out. A criticism you can document is worth more than one you cannot, and the WEF's own published output is documented enough.

I own nothing, have no privacy, and life has never been better' published by the WEF ahead of the 2016 meeting; her later author's note that it 'merely represented a potential future scenario' intended to 'start a discussion about pros and cons', and the retitling to 'Here's how life could change in my city by the year 2030').
framing_note: This ladder's SUBJECT IS PROVENANCE -- the recognition skill is 'who actually said this, where, and in what form', and every rung must model it. THE RAIL, absolute: 'you'll own nothing and be happy' was WEF-published SPECULATION by a named Danish parliamentarian, not a secret plan, not a leak, and not Schwab's sentence. Any rung whose stem or answer implies a leaked plan is a factual error and must be rejected at gate; the bank's credibility on every other contested topic rides on getting this one exactly right, and getting it right is MORE damaging to the WEF than the myth is, because the real thing is signed and citable. SECOND RAIL: the T5 rung correcting the Schwab-father-Nazi rumour is MANDATORY and the bank must never repeat that claim as fact. THIRD RAIL: no cartoon villain and no hagiography -- Schwab is an engineering professor with a published thesis, and the documented record (a book you can buy, a programme you can read) carries the weight without embellishment. VERIFY BEFORE SEEDING: (a) the widely circulated WEF video '8 predictions for the world in 2030' is a separate artefact from Auken's essay and was NOT verified at spec time -- verify its existence, date and exact wording or build the rungs on the essay alone; (b) the 2025 whistleblower allegations and Schwab's April 2025 resignation are entangled with a WEF investigation that reportedly cleared him in August 2025 -- either state both directions or, better, leave the episode out entirely; it adds nothing a kid needs. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the most-quoted sentence about the future was written by a Danish MP as a thought experiment). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent institutions and real people who are genuinely confusable -- the Bilderberg Group, the Trilateral Commission, the Club of Rome, the OECD, the IMF; Thierry Malleret, Ida Auken, Peter Vanham, Christine Lagarde, Henry Kissinger; real WEF book titles and real years. Never a joke option and never an invented organisation. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem mention a Danish politician before asking who wrote the sentence. LANE: HISTORY owns post-war international institutions; ECONOMICS owns stakeholder capitalism and ESG; SCIENCE keeps the Fourth Industrial Revolution's TECHNOLOGY claims and the provenance skill itself.

name: Harari's documented sentences
scope: What one influential futurist actually wrote, quoted exactly, with the venue attached. T3: the historian who became a futurist -- Yuval Noah Harari took an Oxford doctorate on Renaissance military memoirs and teaches medieval and military history at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem; then Sapiens (2011) and Homo Deus (2016) sold tens of millions of copies and made him a fixture at Davos. T3: THE PHRASE -- in an essay published on 24 February 2017, drawn from Homo Deus, Harari named a coming 'useless class': people who would be, in his words, not merely unemployed but UNEMPLOYABLE. T4: his own definition, verbatim -- a class 'devoid of any economic, political or even artistic value, who contribute nothing to the prosperity, power and glory of society'. Read the nouns: value, contribution, prosperity, power, glory. Every one of them measures a person by output. T4: the question he set for economics, verbatim -- 'What should we do with all the superfluous people, once we have highly intelligent non-conscious algorithms that can do almost everything better than humans?' T4: on free will -- speaking at Google on 18 January 2019, he argued that liberal democracy rests on eighteenth-century philosophical ideas, 'especially the idea of free will', and that until now humans were so complicated that 'from a practical perspective, it still made sense to believe in free will'. The claim is not that free will is real or unreal but that believing in it was a useful approximation now expiring. T4: what he thinks ends the approximation -- the merger of information technology with biotechnology, moving surveillance, in his phrase from the same talk, 'under the skin' by way of biometric sensors that read the body rather than the phone. T5: warning or programme? -- Harari presents these as dangers he is describing, and says so; his critics answer that describing human beings as 'superfluous' in the vocabulary of surplus inventory is itself the turn, whatever the intent. Both readings are on the record. Show the kid the sentence and ask what follows from it -- do not answer for them. T5: the check on the sage -- historians and neuroscientists have criticised Harari's books for factual errors and for reducing minds to algorithms. A book that sells tens of millions of copies has passed no test that a paper in a journal has to pass, and the bank applies the same standard to bestsellers that it applies to institutions.
source: ideas.ted.com, Yuval Noah Harari, 'The rise of the useless class', 24 February 2017, excerpted from Homo Deus -- verbatim: 'devoid of any economic, political or even artistic value, who contribute nothing to the prosperity, power and glory of society'; the unemployed/'unemployable' distinction; 'What should we do with all the superfluous people, once we have highly intelligent non-conscious algorithms that can do almost everything better than humans?'; and '99 percent of human qualities and abilities are simply redundant for the performance of most modern jobs'. Transcript of 'Yuval Noah Harari: 21 Lessons for the 21st Century' at Talks at Google, 18 January 2019 -- verbatim on free will as an eighteenth-century inheritance, 'up till now in history, the humans were so complicated that from a practical perspective, it still made sense to believe in free will', and the infotech/biotech merger going 'under the skin' via biometric sensors. Grokipedia 'Yuval Noah Harari' (read via browser) -- Oxford DPhil 2002 on Renaissance military memoirs; Hebrew University post; Sapiens 2011/2014 and Homo Deus 2016; his critique of liberal humanism's free will as illusory under biochemical determinism; and the documented scholarly rebukes from historians and neuroscientists for factual errors and reductionism. Wikipedia 'Yuval Noah Harari' (2016 Davos remarks on a division between 'a superelite of improved humans and a mass of useless people' and on power resting with those who control the algorithms).
framing_note: A pure QUOTE-PROVENANCE ladder -- its whole value is that every sentence is exact and carries a venue and a date. THE RAIL, absolute: no paraphrase may be presented as a quotation, and every quoted rung must name where and when it was said or written. CRITICAL -- the seed phrase 'humans are now hackable animals' was NOT verifiable to a primary transcript at spec time. The build MUST verify its exact wording and venue against the WEF Davos 2020 special address 'How to Survive the 21st Century' (24 January 2020) or another primary transcript before any rung uses it; if verification fails, the rung is CUT and the verified quotes above are used instead. An unsourced quotation in this ladder is a hard fail, not a style note. SECOND RAIL: Harari frames the 'useless class' as a danger he foresees, not a policy he endorses -- no rung may claim he WANTS it, and the T5 rung exists precisely to lay out both readings and hand the judgement to the reader. PRESENT, never preach: the quotations are damning enough to a kid who reads them carefully, and any editorial adjective ('chilling', 'sinister') weakens them. THIRD RAIL: no mockery of the man; he is a serious and widely read scholar whose critics are also named. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (a bestselling historian coined a name for people the economy will not need) and T4 (the verbatim definition, which lands hardest unadorned). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent thinkers and their real phrases, which are richly confusable -- Ray Kurzweil's singularity, Nick Bostrom's superintelligence, Klaus Schwab's Fourth Industrial Revolution, Shoshana Zuboff's 'surveillance capitalism', Jaron Lanier, Ida Auken; and Harari's own real book titles (Sapiens, Homo Deus, 21 Lessons, Nexus) as distractors for which text a line came from. Never invent a quotation for a distractor -- use real quotations by the wrong author. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem gloss 'people the economy cannot use' before asking for the term. LANE, strict: the AI bank owns AI capability claims, automation forecasts and algorithmic mechanics ENTIRELY -- this ladder never adjudicates whether AI can actually do what Harari says, only what he said and where. PHILOSOPHY owns free will as a philosophical problem; science keeps the provenance skill.
history_overlap: AI bank -- near-certain overlap: Harari, the 'useless class', automation-driven unemployment and algorithmic control are natural AI-bank topics. This ladder must key PROVENANCE (which text, which venue, which year, what exact words) and must not argue AI capability, which is the AI bank's alone. PHILOSOPHY bank -- free will and determinism as a philosophical question; this ladder quotes Harari's position and does not re-argue the problem. Within this sub-strand, flag against the Davos ladder (shared WEF setting) and the transhumanism ladder (shared post-human theme): Harari's own sentences belong only here.

name: Transhumanism: a programme, not a prophecy
scope: An ideology with named authors, dated claims and a traceable pedigree. T2: the word has an author -- the biologist Julian Huxley gave 'transhumanism' its modern meaning in a 1957 essay, defining it as the idea that the human species 'can, if it wishes, transcend itself'. T2: WHO HUXLEY ALSO WAS -- across the same decades he was an officer of the British Eugenics Society: vice-president from 1937 to 1944 and its PRESIDENT from 1959 to 1962, and he gave the Galton memorial lecture in 1936 and again in 1962. He was also the first Director-General of UNESCO, from 1946 to 1948, and Aldous Huxley's older brother. The same man, the same years, both ideas. T3: Huxley's own analogy, in his words -- 'no one doubts the wisdom of managing the germ plasm of agricultural stocks, so why not apply the same concept to human stocks?' The phrase to notice is 'human stocks'. T3: the movement organised itself -- Max More wrote the Principles of Extropy in 1990 and founded the Extropy Institute in 1992; Nick Bostrom and David Pearce founded the World Transhumanist Association in 1998, which renamed itself Humanity+ in 2008. Earlier, from 1966, the futurist FM-2030 had used 'transhuman' for people he saw as transitional to a post-human condition. T3: Ray Kurzweil put DATES on it -- The Singularity Is Near (2005) predicted human-level machine intelligence around 2029 and the singularity itself in 2045, and he reaffirmed both in The Singularity Is Nearer in 2024. T4: his actual argument, stated at full strength -- the 'law of accelerating returns': computing power has grown exponentially across five entirely different underlying technologies, from electromechanical machines and relays through vacuum tubes, transistors and integrated circuits, so the trend belongs to the paradigm rather than to any one chip and should survive the death of any one of them. T4: the standing objections, by name -- Paul Allen's 'complexity brake', the argument that understanding intelligence gets harder rather than easier as you advance; Theodore Modis's charge that Kurzweil mistakes logistic curves for exponential ones and sees illusory knees in his own data; and Steven Pinker in 2008: 'There is not the slightest reason to believe in a coming singularity.' T4: why a dated prediction is a gift -- 2029 and 2045 are falsifiable in a way that 'the future will be transformed' never is. Kurzweil, unlike most prophets in this sub-strand, has agreed to be graded, and that deserves saying out loud. T5: the criticism that bites hardest -- that transhumanism is eugenics rewritten in the vocabulary of individual choice, sorting better from worse humans by market rather than by mandate. Huxley's own biography is why the charge is difficult to wave away. T5: the distinction the bank insists on -- repairing a body that is failing is medicine and is celebrated here without reservation (sickle-cell gene therapy, an artificial hip, insulin); declaring a healthy human obsolete and requiring an upgrade is a claim about who deserves to exist, and no experiment can settle that question. A technology is a choice somebody makes, never a destiny that arrives.
source: Wikipedia 'Transhumanism' (Julian Huxley popularising the term in a 1957 essay and the 'can, if it wishes, transcend itself' formulation; W. D. Lighthall's earlier 1940 use; FM-2030's 'transhuman' from 1966 and the 1973 Upwingers Manifesto; Max More's Principles of Extropy 1990, Extropy Magazine 1988 and the Extropy Institute 1992; the World Transhumanist Association founded 1998 by Nick Bostrom and David Pearce, renamed Humanity+ in 2008; and the recorded critique that transhumanism revives eugenic ideology under the banner of individual choice). Wikipedia 'Julian Huxley' (vice-president of the British Eugenics Society 1937-1944 and president 1959-1962; Galton memorial lectures 1936 and 1962; first Director-General of UNESCO 1946-1948; the verbatim 'germ plasm of agricultural stocks ... human stocks' argument; Aldous Huxley his younger brother). Wikipedia 'Technological singularity' (The Age of Spiritual Machines 1999, The Singularity Is Near 2005 with human-level AI around 2029 and the singularity in 2045, reaffirmed in The Singularity Is Nearer 2024; the law of accelerating returns across paradigms; Paul Allen's complexity brake; Theodore Modis on logistic versus exponential curves; Steven Pinker's 2008 'not the slightest reason' remark).
framing_note: The sub-strand's IDEOLOGY ladder, and its spine is a single documented biographical fact: the man who named transhumanism ran the British Eugenics Society. That is not innuendo, it is a date range, and it is why this ladder can make its argument without ever raising its voice. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) Huxley POPULARISED the term and gave it its modern meaning -- he did not coin it outright, since W. D. Lighthall used the word in 1940; write 'popularised', not 'invented'; (2) the Eugenics Society dates are exact and must stay exact -- vice-president 1937-1944, president 1959-1962 -- never rounded into 'he ran it his whole life'; (3) Kurzweil's law of accelerating returns must be presented as a real argument with real evidence before the objections land, because a strawman here would betray the bank's own rule about steel-manning. VERIFY BEFORE SEEDING: (a) Vernor Vinge's 1993 paper 'The Coming Technological Singularity' and its thirty-year horizon -- a strong rung but unverified at spec time; (b) Francis Fukuyama's description of transhumanism as the world's most dangerous idea (Foreign Policy, 2004) -- same status; verify both or omit. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (the founder of transhumanism was simultaneously president of the eugenics society) and T4 (Pinker's flat sentence). DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent figures who are genuinely confusable -- Nick Bostrom, David Pearce, Max More, FM-2030, Aubrey de Grey, Vernor Vinge, Hans Moravec, Marvin Minsky; real adjacent movements -- extropianism, cryonics, mind uploading, the rationalist subculture, effective altruism; and the real Huxley family (Aldous, author of Brave New World; T. H. Huxley, 'Darwin's bulldog') as the richest distractor set in the ladder. Real wrong years for 2029 and 2045. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem mention eugenics before asking what else Julian Huxley presided over -- name him as the man who gave transhumanism its meaning, and let the second office be recalled knowledge. TONE: no cartoon villainy and no horror-movie register; the T5 medicine-versus-obsolescence distinction is the ladder's moral payload and must be stated once, calmly, and not repeated. LANE: the AI bank owns AI capability, timelines and alignment ENTIRELY -- take from Kurzweil only the falsifiability angle; this bank's own eugenics dark-chapters ladder owns Buck v. Bell, Cold Spring Harbor and T4, and this ladder must key HUXLEY'S personal bridge alone.

name: Nullius in verba: take nobody's word for it
scope: The oldest instruction in organised science, and the virtue underneath it. T1: the world's oldest continuously running scientific society, founded in London in 1660, has carried the same three-word motto since the 1660s, and it means 'take nobody's word for it'. T2: the words are borrowed from a poet -- a line of Horace from the Epistles, in which the writer declares himself not bound to swear allegiance to the words of any master. John Evelyn was among the Fellows who chose it. T2: the Society's own gloss on why -- the motto records the Fellows' determination 'to withstand the domination of authority and to verify all statements by an appeal to facts determined by experiment'. That was written down in the 1660s, roughly three and a half centuries before anyone was told to trust the science. T3: the same virtue restated in modern English -- Richard Feynman told Caltech's graduating class in 1974 that 'the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.' Notice the target: not the liar, not the rival, YOU. T4: what Feynman meant by 'cargo cult science' in that address -- research that reproduces the outward FORM of science, the laboratories and papers and graphs and conferences, while omitting the one step that makes it science: the deliberate, unwelcome effort to find out whether you are wrong. T5: the practical test a kid can run on any claim, from any source, including this bank -- ask what evidence would change the speaker's mind. A claim that arrives with an argument and a way to check it is doing science; a claim that arrives with a demand for deference is doing something else, whoever is making it and however correct it may eventually turn out to be.
source: Wikipedia 'Nullius in verba' (the Royal Society founded 1660 and the motto adopted soon after, with John Evelyn among the Fellows who chose it; the source line from Horace, Epistles Book I Epistle I, lines 14-15, 'Nullius addictus iurare in verba magistri, quo me cumque rapit tempestas, deferor hospes'; the Royal Society's rendering 'Not bound to swear by the words of a master; where the storm drives me I turn in for shelter'; and the Society's own published statement that the motto expresses 'the determination of Fellows to withstand the domination of authority and to verify all statements by an appeal to facts determined by experiment'). Richard Feynman, 'Cargo Cult Science', Caltech commencement address, 1974 -- 'The first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool' (also quoted in the science bank's own voice_rule in bankbuild/subjects/science.json).
framing_note: This is the sub-strand's CAPSTONE and the bank's core recognition skill, and per the brief it is stated ONCE, plainly, and POSITIVELY -- it teaches the scientific tradition's OWN motto and Feynman's own words rather than attacking anybody. HARD TONE RAIL: this ladder must name NO living figure, NO current institution and NO current dispute; the moment it reaches for a contemporary example it becomes a sermon and loses everything. There is a no_trust_the_science gate in tools/quizgen/gates/science.py -- the phrase must never appear approvingly, and the T2 rung's contrast is made by CHRONOLOGY (the 1660s versus now), not by naming a target. The Royal Society and Feynman carry the whole load. ACCURACY RAILS: (1) the motto is a motto adopted in the 1660s by Fellows including John Evelyn -- do not assign it a single named inventor or a falsely precise year; (2) distinguish the two translations explicitly -- the literal Horace line is 'not bound to swear by the words of a master', while 'take nobody's word for it' is the Royal Society's own modern rendering, not a literal translation, and a rung that blurs them is teaching sloppiness inside a ladder about rigour; (3) VERIFY Feynman's cargo-cult phrasing and the South Pacific runway image against the 1974 Caltech address before seeding T4. Dinner-test payoff: T1 (a 360-year-old motto that translates as 'take nobody's word for it') -- this is also the ladder's T1-T2 wonder load, and the rung should land as delight, not as warning. DISTRACTOR MINE: unusually rich and entirely real -- rival scientific bodies (the Academie des Sciences, the Accademia dei Lincei, the Invisible College, the Lunar Society) and rival Latin tags with real provenance ('Ipse dixit', 'Cogito ergo sum', Newton's 'Hypotheses non fingo', Bacon's Novum Organum). Real poets other than Horace. Never a joke option. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem translate the motto before asking whose it is. LANE: PHILOSOPHY owns Popper, falsification as epistemology and the demarcation problem; SCIENCE keeps falsification as WORKING PRACTICE -- what a good test actually looks like and the question you can ask of any speaker. HISTORY owns the Royal Society as a Restoration institution.
history_overlap: PHILOSOPHY bank -- Popper, falsifiability and the demarcation problem are certain philosophy topics; this ladder must stay on the practical test ('what evidence would change your mind?') and never argue demarcation. HISTORY bank -- the Royal Society and the Restoration. Within this science bank, flag against any other Feynman ladder (Challenger O-ring, the double slit, safe-cracking): the 1974 cargo-cult address belongs here and must not be duplicated there.
